title: The Planets
hook: Seven planets as seven characters, from the war machine of Mars to a hidden choir that fades into silence.

painting.title: Astronomical Observations: Jupiter
painting.pairingNote: Two astronomers under a night sky turn a long telescope towards Jupiter, its stripes and moons plainly visible; one of eight small canvases of the Sun, the Moon, the planets known in 1711 and a comet.

facts: In the spring of 1913 Holst spent a holiday in Spain with the writer Clifford Bax, who introduced him to astrology. Holst called it his “pet vice” and cast his friends’ horoscopes. *The Planets* is about the planets’ characters in astrology, not about astronomy: each one “brings” something, war, peace, jollity, old age.
He wrote it between 1914 and 1916 and finished the orchestration in 1917. Earth is left out, and Pluto had not been discovered. Holst called the movements “a series of mood pictures”.
The orchestra is huge: six horns, four trumpets, a tenor tuba, two timpani players, celesta, organ, two harps, and in the last movement a choir of women’s voices, out of sight.

Adrian Boult conducted the first performance on 29 September 1918 in the Queen’s Hall, London, for about 250 invited guests; Holst’s friend Balfour Gardiner paid for it. The first complete public performance came in November 1920. The work made Holst famous, and the fame made him uneasy for the rest of his life.
bigPicture.inOneLine: war (I), peace (II), a quicksilver messenger (III), a festival (IV), old age (V), a magician (VI) and a mystic who disappears into silence (VII).

movements.heading: Mars, the Bringer of War
movements.title: Mars, the Bringer of War
movements.summary: A march that cannot march: it has five beats to the bar instead of two or four, and the hammering rhythm never lets go. It starts very quietly and grows into one of the loudest, most dissonant climaxes in the orchestral repertoire. Holst wrote it in mid-1914, before the First World War broke out, but it has been heard as a picture of mechanised war ever since.

mainIdeas.name: The rhythm
mainIdeas.description: a five-beat pattern, tapped out by strings hitting the strings with the wood of the bow, harp and timpani.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a slow, rising line in the low brass and woodwinds that climbs a few notes and slides back.

mainIdeas.name: The fanfare
mainIdeas.description: a call in the tenor tuba, answered by trumpets, in the quieter middle.

stops.hear: A dry, tapping five-beat rhythm, very quiet, in strings, harp and timpani
stops.happening: The strings play [[col-legno|col legno]], with the wood of the bow. The rhythm is an [[ostinato|ostinato]]

stops.hear: Low bassoons and horns play a slow theme that creeps upwards
stops.happening: The main theme, under the rhythm

stops.hear: The theme rises to the brass, louder and louder, to a crushing, clashing chord
The music changes gear: long, sustained chords in the strings and woodwinds
stops.happening: A middle section, in long notes

stops.hear: A lone brass call, answered by trumpets with a quick, sharp figure
stops.happening: The tenor tuba’s fanfare and the trumpets’ reply

stops.hear: The tapping rhythm returns and the opening theme starts its climb again
The whole orchestra hammers the rhythm at full strength; the harmony grinds
stops.happening: The great climax, *ffff* in the score

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Huge, separated chords, then the rhythm pounded out in unison and a final crash
stops.happening: The end: the machine stamps itself out

notice: Try to march to it. You cannot: the fifth beat always gets in the way, which is why the music feels so relentless and so wrong.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Charles Dutoit recorded *The Planets* with the Montreal Symphony Orchestra in 1986 in the church of Saint-Eustache, Montreal. The album won the 1987 Gramophone Award for engineering. The seven movements are tracks 1–7.

movements.heading: Venus, the Bringer of Peace
movements.title: Venus, the Bringer of Peace
movements.summary: After the war, stillness. A horn asks a quiet question, flutes and oboes answer, and harps and celesta rock gently underneath. The middle brings a warm violin melody and a tender oboe solo; then the opening returns, more transparent than before.

mainIdeas.name: The horn call
mainIdeas.description: four rising notes, very soft, answered by falling chords in the woodwinds.

mainIdeas.name: The violin melody
mainIdeas.description: a high, singing line, first for a solo violin and later for all the violins.

mainIdeas.name: The oboe solo
mainIdeas.description: a long, romantic tune at the heart of the movement.

stops.hear: A solo horn plays a slow rising phrase; flutes and oboes answer softly
stops.happening: The opening, *Adagio*: the answer to Mars

stops.hear: Rocking chords in flutes and harps, with a sprinkle of celesta
stops.happening: The gently swaying accompaniment that runs through the movement

stops.hear: A solo violin sings high above the orchestra
The music moves a little faster; the violins share a warm melody over softly offbeat woodwinds
stops.happening: The middle section, *Andante*, in three beats

stops.hear: A single oboe plays a long, tender melody
stops.happening: The central *Largo*: the most romantic tune in the work

stops.hear: The horn call returns, then the solo violin

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: High, shimmering chords for harps, celesta and flutes, fading

notice: Listen for the celesta, a keyboard instrument that sounds like small bells. Holst uses it here for a cool, starry light, and it returns in the last movement.

movements.heading: Mercury, the Winged Messenger
movements.title: Mercury, the Winged Messenger
movements.summary: The shortest movement, a [[scherzo|scherzo]] in quick, flickering notes. Little figures dart from instrument to instrument, often in two keys at once, so the music never quite lands. In the middle a solo violin plays a simple tune, as if the messenger stopped for a moment.

mainIdeas.name: The flicker
mainIdeas.description: a fast, light figure in six beats, thrown between woodwinds and strings.

mainIdeas.name: The tune
mainIdeas.description: a short, folk-like melody, first on a solo violin, high.

stops.hear: Quick, light notes flicker between the woodwinds and the strings
stops.happening: Fragments in two keys set side by side, B-flat major and E major: [[bitonality|bitonality]]

stops.hear: Harp, celesta and glockenspiel add sparkle to the darting figures
A solo violin plays a short, simple tune, high up; the woodwinds take it over
The tune rings out in the whole orchestra, then the flickering returns

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The figures thin out and vanish on a few light notes

notice: Mercury never settles in one key for long. Listen for the moment the solo violin’s tune arrives: it is the only place where the music seems to stand still.

movements.heading: Jupiter, the Bringer of Jollity
movements.title: Jupiter, the Bringer of Jollity
movements.summary: A festival. Bustling strings and six horns set off a string of dance tunes, each bigger than the last. In the middle the music slows to half speed for a broad, noble melody that Holst later turned into a famous hymn. The festivities return, the melody comes back once more, and a final dash ends on a single loud chord.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: busy strings and a bouncing horn tune that pushes against the beat.

mainIdeas.name: The dance tunes
mainIdeas.description: several, one after another, some stamping in three beats.

mainIdeas.name: The big tune
mainIdeas.description: a slow, broad melody, first in the strings and horns. In 1921 Holst set it as the hymn tune “Thaxted”, for the words “I vow to thee, my country”.

stops.hear: Busy, scurrying strings; six horns launch a bouncing, offbeat tune
The whole orchestra joins the tune, loud and bright
A heavier, stamping dance in three beats, in the strings and horns
More tunes, one after another, passed around the orchestra
The music slows; strings and horns sing a broad, noble melody
stops.happening: The *Andante maestoso*, the tune that became “I vow to thee, my country”

stops.hear: The melody rises to a full-orchestra climax
stops.happening: The big tune at full strength

stops.hear: The bustling opening returns
The broad melody returns, grander, but breaks off before it finishes

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A fast rush and one short, very loud chord

notice: When the big tune comes back near the end, listen for how it stops before its last phrase. The final cadence you expect never comes; Holst lets the dance sweep it away.

movements.heading: Saturn, the Bringer of Old Age
movements.title: Saturn, the Bringer of Old Age
movements.summary: Said to have been Holst’s own favourite movement. A slow procession: two chords tick back and forth like a clock while a low line plods beneath them. A solemn melody in the trombones grows into a crushing climax with clanging bells, and then, unexpectedly, peace: old age accepted.

mainIdeas.name: The clock
mainIdeas.description: two soft chords swaying back and forth in flutes, harps and bassoons.

mainIdeas.name: The procession
mainIdeas.description: a slow, heavy tune in the low strings, then a solemn melody in the trombones.

mainIdeas.name: The ending
mainIdeas.description: a calm, high, gently moving music, with harps and flutes.

stops.hear: Two soft chords rocking slowly back and forth; a slow line creeps upwards in the low strings
Trombones play a slow, solemn melody
The melody passes to the whole orchestra; brief, restless outbursts
The ticking turns into a heavy, clanging tread; bells ring out over the full orchestra
The noise dies away; flutes and harps move gently in three slow beats

stops.label: Last 2 minutes
stops.hear: Very quiet, high chords, harps and flutes, fading

notice: Compare the clock at the start with the climax. The same two-chord swing, slow and soft at first, becomes the great tolling of bells.

movements.heading: Uranus, the Magician
movements.title: Uranus, the Magician
movements.summary: Four loud notes in the brass, like a spell, then a clumsy dance in the bassoons that gets more and more out of hand. It reaches a huge climax, with the organ sweeping up and down the keyboard, and suddenly collapses into near silence.

mainIdeas.name: The spell
mainIdeas.description: four slow, loud notes, first in the brass, then in the tubas and the timpani.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a jaunty, galumphing tune in the bassoons, in a heavy six-beat swing.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: a pompous tune in the brass that joins the dance.

stops.hear: Four loud, slow notes in the brass, repeated by the tubas and the timpani
The bassoons start a jaunty, clumsy dance
A loud, swaggering march tune in the brass
stops.happening: The dance swells into a march

stops.hear: The tunes pile up, faster and louder; the four notes keep breaking in
stops.happening: The magic gets out of hand

stops.hear: A huge climax: the organ sweeps up the keyboard, then everything drops to a whisper

stops.label: Last 1:30
stops.hear: Slow, quiet music alternates with brief flashes of the dance, and the four notes fade

notice: If you know Dukas’s *The Sorcerer’s Apprentice*, listen for the family likeness: a spell, bassoons that start a dance and a magic that runs out of control. Whether Holst knew Dukas’s piece is not documented.

movements.heading: Neptune, the Mystic
movements.title: Neptune, the Mystic
movements.summary: The quietest music in the work, from first note to last. Flutes and harps drift in a rocking five-beat motion, chords clash softly, and then women’s voices, singing without words from out of sight, join the orchestra. At the end the orchestra falls silent and the voices fade away as a door between them and the hall is slowly closed.

mainIdeas.name: The drift
mainIdeas.description: soft, swaying figures in flutes, oboes and piccolo.

mainIdeas.name: The chords
mainIdeas.description: two unrelated chords played together by the brass, a cold and strange sound.

mainIdeas.name: The voices
mainIdeas.description: a choir of women, unseen, singing wordless lines.

stops.hear: Flutes play a soft, rocking figure, joined by piccolo and oboes
Quiet brass chords that do not belong together
stops.happening: E minor and G-sharp minor at once

stops.hear: Harps and celesta take over, glittering softly
High women’s voices enter, singing without words, from far away
The orchestra stops; only the voices remain, rocking between two chords

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The voices fade little by little until nothing is left
stops.happening: The fade-out: the score asks for a door to be closed slowly on the singers

notice: Do not stop the music before it ends. The last chord is not resolved, and the voices disappear rather than finish, one of the first fade-outs in music.

threads.title: Astrology, not astronomy
threads.body: The titles come from the planets’ characters in astrology, partly from the writings of the astrologer Alan Leo. Each movement is a mood, not a picture of a planet.

threads.title: The rhythm of five
threads.body: Mars and Neptune, the first and last movements, are both in five beats to the bar: one hammering, the other floating. The same uneven pulse makes war and mystery.

threads.title: Bells and light
threads.body: Celesta, harp and glockenspiel return again and again (Venus, Mercury, Neptune) for a cold, starry glitter, and the bells of Saturn mark the passing of time.

recordings.chorus: Women of the Orchestre symphonique de Montréal Chorus
